blocks.text: The classification of living organisms is organised as a hierarchy, a system of levels, which lets scientists categorise organisms and understand the relationships between different forms of life. Each level is called a taxon (plural: taxa) and represents one rank in the biological classification system. The primary levels of the hierarchy are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species, and above kingdom sits the domain.

blocks.title: Taxon and taxonomic hierarchy
blocks.text: A taxon is one rank, or level, in biological classification, such as a family or a genus. The taxonomic hierarchy is the ordered series of these ranks, from the broadest (domain) to the most specific (species). Moving down the hierarchy, each group contains organisms that share more and more features.

blocks.alt: Eight nested boxes, each inside the one above it, labelled from the outside in: Domain (All organisms), Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
blocks.caption: The taxonomic hierarchy: every rank sits inside the rank above it (original diagram after Figure 1.5).
blocks.long_description: Domain is the outermost box and holds all organisms. Inside it is kingdom, then phylum, class, order, family and genus. Species is the innermost box: a single kind of organism.

blocks.text: The ranks, one by one
1. Domain
Domain is the highest level of classification. Currently there are three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
2. Kingdom

Kingdom is one of the highest taxonomic ranks, just below domain. It groups together all forms of life that share fundamental characteristics. Example: in domain Eukarya there are several kingdoms, such as Animalia (animals), Plantae (plants), Fungi (fungi) and Protista (protists).
3. Phylum

Phylum is the next level below kingdom. Organisms within a phylum share a basic body plan and significant structural features. Example: in kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata includes all animals with a notochord, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
4. Class

Class further divides the organisms of a phylum on the basis of more specific common traits. Example: within phylum Chordata, class Mammalia includes all mammals, which are characterised by having hair and mammary glands.
5. Order

Order categorises organisms within a class on the basis of additional shared characteristics and evolutionary history. Example: within class Mammalia, order Primates includes humans, monkeys and apes, characterised by their large brains and opposable thumbs.
6. Family

Family groups organisms within an order that are even more closely related and share more precise common attributes. Example: within order Primates, family Hominidae includes the great apes and humans.
7. Genus

Genus is a more specific rank within a family. It groups species that are very closely related and often look similar. Example: within family Hominidae, genus Homo includes humans and our closest extinct relatives.
8. Species

Species is the most specific level of classification and represents a single type of organism. Members of a species can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. Example: within genus Homo, the species Homo sapiens refers to modern humans.

blocks.caption: Taxonomic ranks of a human, a sparrow and an onion

blocks.title: Reading a classification
blocks.problem: Which two of the three organisms are most closely related, and at which rank do they stop sharing a group?
steps: Compare the columns from the top. Human, sparrow and onion all belong to domain Eukarya.
At kingdom, the human and the sparrow are both Animalia; the onion is Plantae. So the onion is the least related.
The human and the sparrow are both in phylum Chordata, but at class the human is Mammalia and the sparrow is Aves.
blocks.answer: The human and the sparrow are the most closely related. They share the same domain, kingdom and phylum, and separate at the rank of class.
